title: The age of revolutions
intro: From the American Revolution to the Congress of Vienna: French support for a rebellion, the debt it left the monarchy, a revolution and its terror, an emperor who crowned himself, and the coalitions and the congress that set out to balance Europe again.
end: Thirteen colonies of 2.4 million won with a great power's money, arms and fleet; the war raised that power's debt to about 3.3 billion livres, and by 1788 half its revenue went on servicing it; its revolution turned the nation into an army; a general was made emperor and crowned himself; Britain's credit paid for much of the coalitions' armies, and at Vienna the powers set out to balance one another. steps.title: Thirteen colonies
steps.text: By 1775 the Thirteen Colonies had 2.4 million people. On 14 June 1775 Congress created the Continental Army from 22,000 troops outside Boston and 5,000 at New York City. About 250,000 Americans served, but never more than 90,000 at any one time.

steps.title: Saratoga
steps.text: At Saratoga, Burgoyne's army of 5,791 men faced about 12,000 colonial troops, and he surrendered it on 17 October 1777. By some estimates up to 90% of the arms the Americans used in the campaign came from France.

steps.title: The French alliance
steps.text: Vergennes persuaded Louis XVI to fund a front company that bought munitions for the Patriots and shipped them in neutral Dutch ships. In February 1778 France signed a Treaty of Alliance with the Americans. By one account it spent 1.3 billion livres supporting them directly.
steps.reading: A gold tie is an alliance at a moment: France to the United States, against Great Britain.

steps.title: The Chesapeake and Yorktown
steps.text: At the Chesapeake de Grasse prepared 24 ships of the line for battle, Graves 19. At Yorktown about 19,000 Franco-American troops, 10,800 of them French (Rochambeau had landed 6,000 in 1780), besieged the British; 8,000 soldiers and 214 guns were captured. The Treaty of Paris was signed on 3 September 1783.

steps.title: The debt
steps.text: One account puts the whole American war at 1,066 million livres, paid with new loans at high interest and no new taxes; another puts France's direct aid to the Americans alone at 1.3 billion. The war raised France's debt to about 3.3 billion livres, and by 1788 half of the state's revenue went on servicing it. The Church held upwards of 7% of France's land and took 150 million livres a year.

steps.text: In 1789 the Estates-General met: 302 deputies for the clergy, 289 for the nobility and 611 for the Third Estate, which stood for about 98% of some 28 million people. The clergy itself numbered 115,000 to 150,000.

steps.title: The Bastille
steps.text: On 14 July 1789 the Bastille, holding only seven inmates, was stormed. The Assembly abolished feudalism, put the Church under state control and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man. On 2 November 1789 the Church's property was nationalised and used to back the assignats.

steps.title: The king's execution
steps.text: On 21 January 1793 Louis XVI, aged 38, was guillotined on the Place de la Révolution. That year Austria, Sardinia, Naples, Prussia, Spain and Great Britain formed the First Coalition against revolutionary France. Marie Antoinette was executed on 16 October 1793.

steps.title: The levée en masse
steps.text: In February 1793 the Convention decreed a levy of about 300,000 men. The Committee of Public Safety was formed on 6 April, and in August the levée en masse drafted all men aged 18 to 25. Between 750,000 and 800,000 were conscripted.

steps.title: The Terror
steps.text: From June 1793 the Terror issued 16,594 official death sentences, 2,639 of them in Paris and 1,366 in the seven weeks after the Law of 22 Prairial. Robespierre and 21 of his followers were then sentenced to death under the same law without a hearing; he was executed on 28 July 1794.

steps.text: On 9 November 1799 the bloodless coup of 18 Brumaire overthrew the Directory and replaced it with the Consulate, Bonaparte's regime. A plebiscite approved its constitution on 7 February 1800.

steps.title: The emperor crowns himself
steps.text: Under the Concordat of 1801 the Pope recognised Bonaparte's regime and the regime recognised Catholicism as the religion of the great majority. In 1804 a plebiscite confirmed a hereditary empire: 3.5 million yes, the count inflated by 300,000 to 500,000. On 2 December 1804, at Notre-Dame, with Pope Pius VII present, Napoleon crowned himself. Britain, Russia, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire refused to recognise the title.
steps.reading: The empire's ring: legitimacy (a plebiscite, a Pope at the coronation, the Concordat) and, from 1806, the Continental System.

steps.title: Trafalgar
steps.text: Britain declared war on France in May 1803 and repeatedly financed France's enemies. In April 1805 it formed the Third Coalition with Austria and Russia. After 1793 it raised its sailors from 15,000 to 133,000. At Trafalgar, Nelson's 27 ships of the line met 33 French and Spanish; 18 were captured or destroyed, and Britain lost none.
steps.reading: The Royal Navy's ring: scale, technology and the capital that paid for it.

steps.title: Austerlitz and Jena
steps.text: At Austerlitz Napoleon had some 72,000 men and 157 guns against about 85,000 Allies, 70% of them Russian, with 318 guns. Allied casualties were about 36,000, some 38% of their effective force by a count that puts the army at 89,000. The Prussian army awaiting Napoleon in 1806, about 130,000 with 20,000 Saxons, was decisively defeated at Jena and Auerstedt on 14 October.

steps.title: Europe out of balance
steps.text: The Berlin Decree of 21 November 1806 barred Britain's trade from Europe, hurting France and its allies too. In 1808 Napoleon's Army of Spain, 278,670 men, faced 80,000 raw Spanish troops. In 1812 he deployed 600,000 soldiers against Russia, not counting the Austrian and Prussian contingents; of an original force of 615,000 by another count, only 110,000 came back. Russia's army peaked at 712,000 or 904,000, by two counts.
steps.reading: The dark red lobe beneath the Grande Armée is what it lost in Russia: more than 500,000 men.

steps.title: The alliance against France
steps.text: From 1793 to 1814 Britain paid its allies £46,289,549 in subsidies, which paid for a large share of the Austrian and Russian soldiers, about 450,000 at their 1813 peak. At Leipzig about 560,000 soldiers fought by one count, with 133,000 casualties. In 1815 about 250,000 Frenchmen faced about 850,000 allies; at Waterloo Napoleon's 74,500 met Wellington and 50,000 arriving Prussians. Four days later he abdicated.

steps.title: The Congress of Vienna
steps.text: From September 1814 to June 1815 the Congress of Vienna, chaired by Metternich, set out to resize the main powers so that they would balance each other and remain at peace; the five Great Powers, Austria, Britain, Russia, Prussia and France, dealt behind closed doors. Britain's national debt had reached £679 million. The Concert of Europe, a doctrine of the balance of power, guided European foreign policy until 1914.
steps.reading: The victors' bodies around the Congress: a balance, not a winner.
